Read the run plumbing before answering, so this lands on what already exists.

## The thing to aim at

Babysitting works because you catch two or three moments in a run of forty steps. The rest of the watching is you paying attention so you do not miss those. So the goal is not a nicer window to watch through. It is making those moments findable after they happen and answerable while they are still cheap to answer.

## Most of this is already flowing, drawn in the wrong shape

- The breakdown exists. Every CLI keeps its own list, and `toolActions.ts:86` already folds `todowrite`, `updateplan` and the rest onto one line that says "Planned". The agent hands crew the task broken down, several times a run, and crew prints one word about it and lets it scroll away.
- Steps carry the files they touched with diffs, so what has been built since any point in a run is a number we already hold.
- Steering already lands mid-run, on Claude. `steerable` is the flag, everything else queues.

First move, then: take the list crew is already handed and stand it up, rewritten in place, current item lit, count of what is done against a list that is allowed to grow. No new instructions, no model cooperation, no second call. That alone kills most of the reason to sit and watch.

## Decisions and questions have to be asked for

Those are not in the stream as anything crew can pick out, and I would not try to infer them from steps. Ask the way voice asks: a short brief added to every prompt in the thread the way `PLAN_INSTRUCTIONS` and `VOICE_INSTRUCTIONS` are, plus a small typed card in `src/shared/work.ts` holding the rule `cleanCard` already holds, one with nothing on it is null rather than an empty box. Nothing about the brief is ever a message. `VoiceReply` already does the hard half, parsing a card out of a stream without ever letting a partial one through.

Three kinds is enough. Settled, open, risky.

## The one that matters: a question that does not stop the work

An agent asks itself "shared or server" and answers itself in the same breath. That is the moment you are sitting there for. So: the question opens as a row, the agent takes its own best answer and keeps going, and the row stands there marked as assumed. Answering it is one tap and goes in as a steer.

Not answering costs nothing. Answering early costs nothing. Answering late costs whatever was built on the assumption, and we can say that on the row itself, because we have the files: "two files since this" reads differently from "nine files and a rename". That turns "should I interrupt" from a feeling into a number.

## Aiming a correction at a thing

Every card is something to press. Pressing one opens the composer quoting it, the way `ReplyQuote` works today. "No, key it on the commit" said against the decision is unambiguous. The same sentence typed into the thread three steps later is a guess about what you meant.

## While you were away

This is the payoff of marking them, and it is the opposite of babysitting. Come back to thirty new rows and you do not want to read them, you want the two that changed the shape of the work. Once decisions and questions are cards, that view is free.

## Where it lives

Tucked above the composer, the way `QueueBar` and `GhostBar` already tuck. One line when nothing is open, opens to the whole list. Not a new tab, because the point is that it stands beside the scroll rather than being something you choose over the files you are reading.

## What I would leave out

A second model summarizing the run, which is a second thing to be wrong and a call per step. A progress bar, since the agent does not know how far along it is and a bar that jumps from 40 to 90 teaches people to stop reading it. Confidence numbers, which are a model's number about nothing.

Two honest risks. Cards cost tokens and can tip an agent into performing planning instead of working, which is the same tension plan mode has, so the brief stays one paragraph and never requires a card. And only Claude takes a steer mid-run, so on Codex and the rest an answer joins the queue, which the row has to say rather than being a button that quietly does nothing.

Want me to start with the standing list off the todo tool calls? It needs no brief and no model cooperation, so it is the piece we can look at today and judge the rest against.

I'm running into a couple of test issues with the member photo component. The first one is about the initial state — when I add "Away" text, the test still expects to find ALI's initial "A" and count one "Add a photo" button, plus one image element. The second issue is with the heading lookup — the test is looking for a heading with the text "People", and I'm rendering that as an `<h2>` inside a `<section>`, which should work fine with the role query.

Now there's a problem with the "Where this crew is kept" section that calls `window.crew?.current?.()`. In the test environment, `window.crew` is just `{ agentCapabilities }`, so `current` is undefined. I was worried this would crash when trying to call `.then()` on undefined, but optional chaining actually short-circuits the entire chain — so `window.crew?.current?.().then(setSession)` safely evaluates to undefined without ever reaching the `.then()` call when `current` doesn't exist.

I'm also importing `folderName` and `folderLine` from `views/home/place`, which is a component importing from a view module. It's a bit awkward architecturally, but since it's just a pure helper function living in the views directory, it should be acceptable.

The imports for `Pill`, `CheckGlyph`, `LinkGlyph`, `FolderGlyph`, and `DesktopGlyph` are all being used. The `share` function returns `Promise<string | null>`, and the "Away" label correctly shows disconnected members in the list. The `mono-inline` class is being used for monospace text alongside sans-serif, which works fine.

For the Joining section, I need to handle the case where a non-hosting member can still see and copy the join link they used to invite others, but shouldn't see the toggle for controlling who can join. I'm restructuring the section so it only shows if either hosting is true or a joinLink exists, then conditionally render the toggle only for hosts.

For a non-hosting joiner, `window.crew.current()` returns their session with the `home` property pointing to their local folder where they cloned or opened the project, which is the expected behavior. Let me make those edits now.

Starting with the shared types file, I'm defining the core Subagent interface with properties for identification, metadata, configuration, and timestamps, then creating a validation function to clean and normalize subagent data with optional provider settings and enforced limits.

Now I'm mapping out the API routes for the agent spawning system — endpoints for creating child agents, waiting for their completion, sending messages, stopping execution, and querying their state. I'm deciding on the response shape for spawn, where returning both `id` and `threadId` with the same value keeps the preamble simple while maintaining clarity about what identifier to use.

Defining the Thread interface to track parent relationships, role assignments, subject matter, nesting depth, and notification preferences. Then sketching out the `spawnSubagent` function signature and its initial validation logic to ensure the prompt exists and has active credentials.

Now I'm working through the spawn logic itself — checking depth limits, counting running and total child threads under the parent, resolving the role either by ID or by name (case-insensitive since models are more likely to pass names), picking the agent, creating the child thread, and queuing the prompt. The tricky part is figuring out who the "member" should be for the child prompt — it should be the parent agent's author rather than creating a new member, so I need to construct a Member object from the parent thread's creator. Defining the return coalescing mechanism... Adding protocol fields... The runner's steer signature has a `byName` field for framing, which I'll keep and just branch on depending on whether it's a subagent return. For ghosts, I'm setting up `ghostOf(childThreadId)` so the child inherits the parent's ghost, storing it with the parent's websocket and its own event transcript. When `dropGhosts` runs, it iterates by websocket, so child ghosts get cleaned up automatically since they share the parent's ws. A non-ghost parent spawning a child creates a normal thread instead.

When a parent prompt is cancelled, I need to find all child threads with that `parentPromptId` and cancel their running prompts plus clear their queues. For the `/agents/<id>` GET endpoint, I'm returning state, subject, said, tokens, and files — where files tracks what changed per child thread based on their steps.

To extract the files server-side, I can scan the child thread's `agent.step` events and pull the paths from steps that are edits. Let me check the AgentStep shape in the shared types to understand what I'm working with.

+ import type { AgentSettings } from './llm'
+ 
+ // A subagent is a role: a name, a brief, and how it runs. It belongs to the
+ // crew the way a tool does, so everybody's agents get the same helpers. A run
+ // of one is an ordinary thread with a parent, which is what gives it steps,
+ // thinking, diffs, cancel and a place to be talked to without any of that
+ // having to be invented here.
+ 
+ export interface Subagent {
+   id: string
+   name: string
+   brief: string
+   // The CLI a run of this role would rather have. A role that names none runs
+   // on whoever asked for it, which keeps the common case on one machine.
+   provider?: string
+   settings: AgentSettings
+   createdBy: string
+   ts: number
+ }
+ 
+ export const NAME_LIMIT = 24
+ export const BRIEF_LIMIT = 4000
+ export const SUBJECT_LIMIT = 80
+ export const TASK_LIMIT = 8000
+ export const MAX_SUBAGENTS = 40
+ export const SETTING_LIMIT = 12
+ export const SETTING_VALUE_LIMIT = 120
+ 
+ // How many may run at once under one parent, how many a parent thread may run
+ // through in its life, and how many times one may be woken by a helper coming
+ // back. Without the last of these a parent that spawns on every wake is a loop
+ // the crew watches burn tokens all afternoon.
+ export const FAN_LIMIT = 4
+ export const RUN_LIMIT = 16
+ export const WAKE_LIMIT = 8
+ export const DEPTH_LIMIT = 2
+ 
+ // The longest a parent may park on a wait, and the breath a run of returns is
+ // gathered over. Three helpers finishing together are one interruption, because
+ // three steers into a live turn is three times the model is pulled off what it
+ // was doing.
+ export const WAIT_MS = 60000
+ export const RETURN_COALESCE_MS = 1500
+ 
+ export interface SubagentDraft {
+   name: string
+   brief: string
+   provider?: string
+   settings: AgentSettings
+ }
+ 
+ function cleanSettings(settings: AgentSettings | undefined): AgentSettings {
+   if (!settings || typeof settings !== 'object') return {}
+   const out: AgentSettings = {}
+   for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(settings)) {
+     if (Object.keys(out).length >= SETTING_LIMIT) break
+     if (typeof value !== 'string') continue
+     const name = key.trim().slice(0, NAME_LIMIT)
+     if (!name) continue
+     out[name] = value.trim().slice(0, SETTING_VALUE_LIMIT)
+   }
+   return out
+ }
+ 
+ // What arrives over the wire is whatever the other end sent, so a role is only
+ // as good as this. One with no name, or nothing to say what it is for, is not a
+ // role and comes back as null rather than as a helper that sits there with
+ // nothing to do.
+ export function cleanSubagent(
+   name: string,
+   brief: string,
+   opts: { provider?: string; settings?: AgentSettings } = {}
+ ): SubagentDraft | null {
+   const cleanName = typeof name === 'string' ? name.trim().slice(0, NAME_LIMIT) : ''
+   const cleanBrief = typeof brief === 'string' ? brief.trim().slice(0, BRIEF_LIMIT) : ''
+   if (!cleanName || !cleanBrief) return null
+   const provider = typeof opts.provider === 'string' ? opts.provider.trim().slice(0, NAME_LIMIT) : ''
+   return {
+     name: cleanName,
+     brief: cleanBrief,
+     ...(provider ? { provider } : {}),
+     settings: cleanSettings(opts.settings)
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ // A role is named by a model rather than picked from a list, so it is found by
+ // whatever the model wrote: the id it was given, or the name as a person reads
+ // it, however it happens to be capitalised.
+ export function findSubagent(roles: readonly Subagent[], named: string): Subagent | undefined {
+   const asked = typeof named === 'string' ? named.trim().toLowerCase() : ''
+   if (!asked) return undefined
+   return roles.find(role => role.id.toLowerCase() === asked) ?? roles.find(role => role.name.toLowerCase() === asked)
+ }
+ 
+ export const SUBAGENT_INSTRUCTIONS = [
+   `You are a helper on one piece of work, handed to you by another agent.`,
+   `Do that piece and nothing around it. Nobody is reading over your shoulder, so there is no conversation to keep up and no summary of what you are about to do.`,
+   `Answer with what you found or what you changed, in a few lines. That answer goes back to whoever sent you, so write it for them: findings, file paths, and anything that turned out differently from the task as it was worded.`,
+   `Do not send out helpers of your own unless the task says to.`
+ ].join('\n')
+ 
+ const SPAWN_ROOM = (room: number): string =>
+   room > 0
+     ? `You can have ${room} more running at once.`
+     : `You have as many running as you can have at once. Wait for one to come back before sending another.`
+ 
+ // The words a parent is given. They are written here rather than on the host
+ // because only the machine running the agent knows the address it reaches the
+ // session at, which is the same reason the design board's own preamble is
+ // written where it is.
+ export function subagentPreamble(
+   apiBase: string,
+   promptId: string,
+   roles: readonly Subagent[],
+   room: number
+ ): string | null {
+   if (roles.length === 0) return null
+   return [
+     `## Helpers`,
+     ``,
+     `You can send work out to helpers and keep working while they do it. Each one runs on a real machine here, in this project, on its own.`,
+     ``,
+     `The roles you have:`,
+     ...roles.map(role => `  ${role.name} — ${role.brief.split('\n')[0]}`),
+     ``,
+     `Send one out:`,
+     `  curl -s -X POST ${apiBase}/agents/spawn -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"promptId":"${promptId}","role":"${roles[0].name}","subject":"What it is doing, in a few words","task":"The whole of what it should do, written as if to somebody who cannot see this thread."}'`,
+     `That returns an id straight away. It does not wait.`,
+     ``,
+     `Then carry on with your own work. When a helper finishes, its answer arrives in the middle of what you are doing, the way a message from a person does. You do not poll for it and you do not have to stop.`,
+     ``,
+     `Say something to one that is still going:`,
+     `  curl -s -X POST ${apiBase}/agents/<id>/say -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"promptId":"${promptId}","text":"..."}'`,
+     `Read where one has got to:`,
+     `  curl -s ${apiBase}/agents/<id>`,
+     `Stop one:`,
+     `  curl -s -X POST ${apiBase}/agents/<id>/stop -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"promptId":"${promptId}"}'`,
+     ``,
+     `If you have nothing of your own left to do and would rather park than poll:`,
+     `  curl -s -X POST ${apiBase}/agents/wait -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"promptId":"${promptId}","ids":["<id>"],"ms":${WAIT_MS}}'`,
+     `It comes back after ${Math.round(WAIT_MS / 1000)} seconds whether or not they are done. Prefer working over waiting.`,
+     ``,
+     `How to use them:`,
+     `  Send out work that does not sit on the files you are holding. Two agents editing one file at the same time is the one thing nothing here can merge.`,
+     `  Write the task in full. A helper cannot see this thread, the messages in it, or what you have already worked out.`,
+     `  Say in one line who you sent where, then get on with your own part. Do not narrate what they are doing: that is already on the screen beside your words.`,
+     `  ${SPAWN_ROOM(room)}`,
+     `  Keep the promptId exactly as it is above. It is what says the work is yours.`
+   ].join('\n')
+ }
+ 
+ export interface SubagentReturn {
+   name: string
+   subject: string
+   ok: boolean
+   ms: number
+   text: string
+ }
+ 
+ const spell = (ms: number): string => {
+   const seconds = Math.max(1, Math.round(ms / 1000))
+   if (seconds < 60) return `${seconds}s`
+   const minutes = Math.floor(seconds / 60)
+   const rest = seconds % 60
+   return rest === 0 ? `${minutes}m` : `${minutes}m ${rest}s`
+ }
+ 
+ // What the parent reads when a helper comes back. The host writes the whole of
+ // it rather than the runner framing one, because a breath of returns arrives as
+ // one interruption and there is no single name to frame it under.
+ export function returnText(finished: readonly SubagentReturn[], stillOut: readonly string[]): string {
+   const lines = finished.map(one =>
+     one.ok
+       ? [`${one.name} finished after ${spell(one.ms)} and said:`, one.text.trim() || '(nothing)']
+       : [`${one.name} stopped after ${spell(one.ms)} without finishing:`, one.text.trim() || '(no reason given)']
+   )
+   const out = lines.flatMap((pair, index) => (index === 0 ? pair : ['', ...pair]))
+   if (stillOut.length > 0) {
+     out.push('', stillOut.length === 1 ? `${stillOut[0]} is still going.` : `${stillOut.join(' and ')} are still going.`)
+   }
+   return out.join('\n')
+ }
+

I'm adding a `closedPlans` field to track which plans have been dismissed, then implementing actions like `showPlan` to manage the active plan state and remove items from the closed list when they're reopened.

For the helper functions, I'm creating a utility to extract the threadId from a closed plan tab so I can consistently remember which plans to keep hidden across different close actions—whether it's closing a single tab, hiding a plan, or clearing everything at once. Adding the closePlan helper...

I'm debating whether to rename `hidePlan` to something clearer like `dropPlan` to avoid confusion with `closePlan`, since they serve different purposes — one removes the plan from view when there's no active thread, the other closes the plan tab itself.

For `showPlan`, I need to clear the dismissal state when opening a plan thread so it doesn't stay hidden.

In the effect hook, I'm checking whether the plan thread exists and calling the appropriate method — if it's gone, hide the plan; otherwise, show it if it hasn't been manually closed.

**TabPill:** Removing the pinned state so the pill consistently displays padding, the close button, and context menu options.

**Close button in header:** Simplifying the condition to just check if there are any tabs present rather than filtering by kind.

**ThreadView:** Adding the toggle button to the header, and I'm debating where it should go visually—probably at the end after the counts pill since the plan relates to thread content rather than the run status.

For styling, I'll match it to the "Mark done" button's scale with an h-8 w-8 rounded-full icon button in the same ink-800 color, keeping it consistent with the existing header elements.

The button's appearance changes based on whether the plan is visible — showing a darker background with secondary text when inactive, and brightening on hover. I'm using an active scale transform to give it tactile feedback when pressed, matching the pattern elsewhere in the interface.

The tooltip and aria-label will toggle between "Show plan" and "Hide plan" depending on the current state. For the header width calculation, I'm watching the status group's width so the name field can properly adjust when the button appears or disappears.

One thing to consider: the plan button should only render when there's actually a plan to show. And I'm checking the active tab state to determine if the plan tab is currently selected — if another tab is active, the button appears unlit, and clicking it switches to the plan view. There's a distinction between the side panel being completely closed versus just having a different tab active, which affects how the button behaves.

Now I need to update the test cases to reflect the new behavior where the plan tab closes like any other tab, and the close option appears in the menu.

I should also consider whether to add a separate test for the button in ThreadView, but that would require setting up a lot of store state and ResizeObserver mocking. Let me think about what's actually needed to test this properly.

The simplest approach is to extend the existing thread-view-probe test with a second case that opens a thread containing a plan and toggles the button — this gives us a real integration test where pressing the button makes the plan tab appear and disappear while the thread stays open. The challenge is that the full App setup requires `window.crew` to be initialized, which the current probe doesn't have. I could render ThreadView directly with the necessary store fields instead of using the full App, which keeps the test simpler and more focused. ThreadView needs events, steps, selfId, threads, threadPrompts, tokens, agents, queues, threadDrafts, and pending from the store, plus handling for sessionStorage and member presence.
Now I'll make the change. First the browser store:

step.text:
I'm ready to recommend going with the board approach. It's the right structural fit for breaking down and reviewing work, and it follows the same pattern as the existing plan panel—where `kind: 'plan'` controls visibility through `showPlan`/`hidePlan` and only persists while the thread is active. Adding `kind: 'work'` as another option in that union makes sense.

But there's a real problem with the column layout. Questions and Decisions aren't workflow states—they're not things that move through Todo, Doing, In Review, Done. Putting them as columns means the two most important things end up as the rightmost columns you have to scroll to see, and with the default 480px width, six columns only gives each 70px of space, which is impossible to work with in a side panel. The fix is to keep three flowing columns (Todo, Doing, Done or with In Review) and attach Questions and Decisions directly to the tickets they belong to, since every question and decision is always about a specific ticket. The board's top could then show open questions as a queue since that's what actually needs action.

Though I'm second-guessing myself—a question does move through states (open to answered), so maybe the Questions column works as a queue after all. But it doesn't share the same flow as the task columns, so mixing them feels dishonest about what's actually happening.

I think the cleaner approach is keeping the board strictly for work flow (Todo, Doing, Review, Done), with Questions living above it as a separate strip since they're the only thing with a real deadline. Decisions attach to individual tickets instead, showing the count right there. That way the board stays focused on work, and the urgent stuff isn't buried in a horizontal scroll.

The Review column is actually the linchpin here—it's where the agent hands off a completed piece and you see exactly what changed, rather than wading through forty steps. Everything else lives in the thread.

On `/tickets` as a mode: it shouldn't work like plan, where you toggle it per thread. Plan changes what the agent can do, but tickets should just be available as a view. The crew's todo list and the board need to stay separate—one tracks work requests across the team, the other captures a single run's breakdown—but they can connect through the threadId that's already logged when a todo gets picked up. The trickier question is whether the board itself should persist: run state normally stays ephemeral in the snapshot, but decisions and items in review are things you'd want to come back to, so there's a case for letting tickets ride with the snapshot.

Rather than logging every column move as an event (which would bloat the chat log), I'll store one record per ticket that gets rewritten in place. The first concrete slice is a simple Doing/Todo/Done board built directly from the existing todo tool calls, and the ticket card can also track which files have been touched since it entered Doing—that's the latency cost metric from before. On interaction, humans should be able to drag tickets, but only in specific ways. I need to verify whether the crew system already has a review concept before I tie the "In review" column to it, since there's a RepoReview component and a review count in the interface. Let me check what that actually represents.

step.text: Now the steer path, the run path, and the finish path.

Yes. And the panel already has the slot: a browser tab carries a `kind`, `'plan'` is one of them, and `showPlan`/`hidePlan` in `state/browser.ts` stand it up beside the thread it belongs to and take it down when you leave. A board is `'work'` in that same union. That part is nearly free.

The six columns are where I would push back, for one reason: Questions and Decisions are not stations on the same track. A ticket walks Todo, Doing, In review, Done. A question never walks it and a decision never walks it. Put all six in a row and the board says a ticket travels from Questions into Todo, which it does not, so the two piles that matter most become the two you scroll sideways to. The panel is 480 by default. Six columns is 70 pixels each.

## What I would draw

The board is the flow, three or four columns, and it is the whole width.

Questions stand above it as a strip, because they are the one thing on that screen with a clock on them. Each one already carries the agent's own assumption and a count of what has been built since, so answering is a tap and the row says what late costs. That strip empties, and an empty strip is nothing rather than a column that is always there saying zero.

Decisions hang off the ticket they were made inside. Every decision is about a piece of work, so the ticket is where it belongs, and the card carries a small count you can open. That also gives the "while you were away" read for nothing: the tickets that moved, with the decisions under them.

In review is the column that pays for all of it. Everything else you can already read off the thread. In review is the agent saying this slice is finished, look at it, and pushing it back to Doing with a sentence is a steer aimed at one slice of work rather than a correction typed into a run of forty steps. That drag is the interaction I would build the whole thing around.

## What /tickets should mean

Plan is a mode because it changes what the agent may do: read, write the plan, stop. Tickets change nothing about the work, only what the agent says about it, so I would not gate the board behind a command. Crew is already handed the breakdown several times a run through the todo tool calls, and `toolActions.ts` folds it to one word. Draw the board off that and every thread has one today, without a brief and without model cooperation.

Then `/tickets` is three lines in `SLASH_COMMANDS` and means report as you go: raise a question rather than answering yourself, name a decision when you make one. That is the half that needs a paragraph in the prompt the way plan and voice add theirs.

## Where it is written down

Not as an event per move, or a sync pass carries a `ticket.moved` for every step of every run. One record per ticket, rewritten in place, and the column moves ride in the snapshot the way a call and the music do. Decisions and what went through review are worth keeping, since those are what you come back to.

The crew's todo list stays what it is, people asking for work. `todo.started` already carries a threadId, so a todo somebody picked up opens onto the board of the run doing it.

I would start with the flow columns off the todo calls, no command, no brief, and judge questions and review against something we can look at.

The avatar click should open settings directly instead of a popover menu, which means the entire profile popover gets removed—Invite moves to the People page and Leave stays in the You page within settings. This actually solves the concern about the user popover expanding, since it's replaced by the settings modal entirely.

Now I need to clean up TopBar by removing all the popover-related logic, components, and icons like PhotoPicker, MenuItem, and the various glyphs. The user-menu test will need significant rewriting since it heavily covers the popover behavior, though I should preserve the nav tabs and settings behavior tests. I'm also thinking about MenuItem's word-swap toggle coverage—if the profile menu disappears, I need to make sure that toggle behavior is still tested elsewhere in the app where MenuItem is used. ests for the new settings behavior, and I'll grep to see if any MenuItem still toggles its label—if not, I'll note that the word-swap test is gone but the mechanism itself is still covered elsewhere. On the page transitions, the left/right slide animation feels wrong; I should replace it with a simple fade or fade-up effect instead, keeping the content keyed by tab so it animates smoothly as users switch between sections.

The constraint is that padding needs to stay inside the height to avoid scrollbar flicker—since my page isn't set to min-h-full, a vertical translate would only cause overflow if the content already exceeds the box, adding unwanted scroll distance. So I'll stick with a fade-only animation, no movement, and add a new `animate-fade` keyframe that transitions opacity from 0 to 1 over about 160ms.

Adding fade animation styles...

For the "Add an agent" button, it's currently positioned awkwardly below the list. I'm considering moving it to the title row at the top-right, but that's where the close X button sits, so I need to figure out how to position them without collision.

The best approach mirrors what Notion does: place the X at the very top-right corner and put the "Add agent" button on the title row itself with some right margin to avoid overlap. This gives the layout a cleaner, more intentional feel with the X floating above and the action button integrated into the section header. Instead, I could put an "Add agent" card at the end of the list—a hollow card matching the AgentCard style with a plus icon. This mirrors how the toolbox handles empty states: an empty slot that both invites creation and serves as the empty state itself. It removes the floating button entirely and gives the interface a consistent, object-based feel rather than a random UI element.

For the implementation, I'll refactor CreateAgent to render the hollow card as its trigger instead of the pill button. Since it's only used in one place, the simplest approach is to have CreateAgent own its state and just swap out the trigger markup.

Building the hollow card component... I'm reconsidering the border style — a dashed stroke conflicts with the ghost-thread pattern, so I should switch to a solid faint border matching the AgentCard styling instead. The secondary text about where agents come from feels incomplete, and I'm thinking about making it more informative by conditionally showing different copy when the list is empty, something like explaining you can add agents from your machine's LLMs or wait for someone else to contribute theirs.

I'll pass a `first` prop to the CreateAgent component to track whether it's the only item, then conditionally render that extra explanatory line. The Agents page layout becomes straightforward — just map the sorted agents and include the CreateAgent card at the end.

Now I'm moving on to rewrite the TopBar to handle avatar clicks opening settings instead.

For the avatar button, I'm adding a Tooltip with the label "Settings" since clicking it now opens the settings panel rather than a menu. I'll also update the aria-label from "Profile menu" to "Settings" to match the new behavior, though I need to check what the tests are referencing.

The popover removal is justified — the user explicitly wants the photo to open settings directly. Everything that was in the popover (inviting people, invite link, theme, sounds, leave, identity info) is now accessible elsewhere, though inviting people does require an extra click. step.text:
I'm setting up an integration test where a helper agent responds back into a parent turn, with the parent's steering commands being captured by the fake CLI as `steered:<text>` output. The test will verify that when a subagent is added via `subagent.add` and connected to a steerable runner with a long delay, the interaction flows correctly between parent and child. The issue is that both parent and child use the same delay from the environment, so the parent's turn would finish before the child returns, triggering the requeue path instead of the live-steer path I want to test. I need to assign the child role a different provider — the quick non-steerable one — so the parent runs with a long delay while the child completes faster, keeping the parent's turn open long enough to receive the steer delivery.

For test 1, I'll use a role with `provider: 'fake'` and run the parent on `steery` with a long delay so the child finishes while the parent is still running. Test 2 checks what happens when a child returns to a non-steerable parent: the parent's turn ends and a new silent turn opens on the parent thread with no message event, just a second agent start containing "finished after". Tests 3 and 4 cover multiple children returning as a single steer, and various cap refusals like depth and fan limits. Test 5 starts checking what happens when `say` reaches a running child, `stop` stops it, and `wait` returns pending inside its bound.

I'm also noting that `agent.start.promptText` for the silent turn will be the return text, which is useful for assertions. The `subagentReturn` call from `finishPrompt` emits `subagent.ended` to the ghost websocket, and `deliverReturns` uses `SYSTEM_AUTHOR_NAME` as the byName, so `agent.start.byName` will be 'crew'. There's a subtle bug I'm tracking: in `finishPrompt`, the thread is looked up from the prompt's threadId before the prompt gets deleted.

The real issue is when a child finishes and `subagentReturn` fires, it can wake the parent whose run was just cancelled, causing `deliverReturns` to requeue a silent prompt onto the parent thread and start a new turn on something that should be stopped. The fix is to set `thread.notify = false` in `stopSubagent` before cancelling.

I also need to handle the case where `waitSubagents` calls `settled()` which tries to access a thread that might have been deleted, and fix `subagentState` to compute tokens for the specific child's run rather than the agent's total.

There's a known macOS issue with `-webkit-app-region: drag` in Electron where the drag regions become stale after layout changes, and child elements marked as `no-drag` don't always get respected when nested inside `drag` parents. The core problem is that these regions don't recalculate when elements move or change without triggering a repaint of the drag area itself.

Looking at the actual code structure, the `TopBar` is marked as draggable, with the nav and right-side controls marked as non-draggable, and the `CrewLogo` also carries the no-drag flag. The issue is likely that when the layout shifts (like in compact mode), the drag region cache doesn't update properly, leaving some header elements stuck in the draggable zone. The `ResizeObserver` triggering a `compact` state change that shifts the layout width could leave the draggable region stale if it's not recomputed afterward, putting buttons in the wrong hit area. But there's a more specific Electron macOS issue at play here: the draggable region implementation uses an NSView overlay that can swallow clicks if the region isn't properly synchronized with the actual layout. Let me check the Electron version and look for known issues around this. ily test click behavior. Let me check the git history and Electron version to see if there's prior work on this issue. The header is `h-70px` with traffic lights positioned at `{ x: 20, y: 27 }`, but on macOS with `hiddenInset`, the system titlebar still occupies the top ~28px across the full width — and even though Electron applies `NSWindowStyleMaskFullSizeContentView`, clicks in that band might still be intercepted by the titlebar view rather than reaching the web content.

This could explain the exact problem: with buttons spanning y=15 to y=55, the top 28px band overlaps the upper 13px of every header button, making the top portion of tabs and avatars unclickable while the lower part responds normally. Let me verify if this theory holds. why double-clicking triggers window zoom and dragging moves it. Electron handles this differently by making the titlebar transparent and using Chromium's draggable region system, which creates a drag region view covering the entire window with exclusion subviews for non-draggable areas.

The drag region's `hitTest` method returns nil for points inside exclusion rects to let events pass through to the web contents, otherwise it returns self to drag the window. If those cached rects become stale, clicks fall through to the drag overlay and get swallowed—which is exactly the "sometimes I can't click the header elements" problem.

The rects go stale when `UpdateDraggableRegions` isn't called after layout changes. Chromium only sends `DraggableRegionsChanged` when the draggable region set actually changes during paint/layout, so if the header's layout shifts due to a badge appearing, the presence stack changing width, connection text appearing or disappearing, or compact mode toggling, the cached rects don't update.

There's also a known Electron bug where draggable regions aren't recomputed on window resize, leaving the exclusion rects in their old positions. Rather than keep speculating, I should actually diagnose this: check the Electron version, examine what's layered above TopBar to see if anything is overlaying it with `app-drag` styling or covering the drag region, and trace through when the rects actually get recomputed versus when layout changes occur.

Looking at the specific code structure, there's a Boot overlay with `app-drag absolute inset-0` that only shows once, and a TasksPanel positioned absolutely on the right with `pointer-events-auto` inside what's presumably a `pointer-events-none` container. The tricky part is that `-webkit-app-region` ignores pointer-events entirely — an element marked `no-drag` or `drag` still affects the drag region even if it has `pointer-events: none`. The TasksPanel has `app-no-drag` which should exclude it, but I need to verify whether the parent overlay's pointer-events state is interfering with the actual drag rect calculation.

Let me check App.tsx to see what's layered above the TopBar and look for any full-screen overlays that might be creating unexpected drag regions.

The issue is that `import.meta.env.DEV` evaluates to false during vitest because the shell sets NODE_ENV=production when resolving the config, which is a known problem from Jamel's profile setup. This causes `bootSeen()` to always return false and `rememberBoot()` to do nothing, so the App component always renders the Boot screen in tests. The root cause traces back to that NODE_ENV=production export breaking the dev/test environment detection logic.

With DEV false, `bootSeen` is hardcoded false and there's no way to bypass the flight sequence from a test. These tests were passing before the boot work landed, so this is a genuine regression — in production with DEV false, the flight always plays by design. Under vitest, the boot's `onDone` callback never fires because canvas animations don't actually run in jsdom (getContext is missing), so the app never appears and tests hang. I'm weighing options to fix this, starting with...

The cleanest approach might be to leverage reduced motion: if Boot checks `prefers-reduced-motion` and lands immediately when it's enabled, tests could stub `matchMedia` to return matches: true and bypass the animation entirely. jsdom doesn't implement matchMedia by default, so tests could define it themselves. Let me check how Boot.tsx actually handles reduced motion to see if this would work.

+

+     for (const runner of runners) runner.close()

The issue is that the boot process relies on timers—it waits for LANDED (1600ms) then GONE (360ms) before calling onDone—but the tests render synchronously and assert immediately, so they fail before those timers fire. I'm considering two approaches: either mock `matchMedia` to return `still` true so `landed` triggers immediately on mount, or find another way to bypass the async timer chain in tests.

The real insight is that `bootSeen()` gates on DEV mode as a development convenience—in tests we want it to never fly at all. Rather than adding test-only branches to product code or making every test use `waitFor`, I'm thinking the cleanest approach is to have the test helper stub `matchMedia` and handle the timer logic there. Writing test helper...

The idea is to wrap the initial render in a helper that temporarily switches to fake timers, advances past the 360ms animation window, then switches back to real timers — keeping the fake timer switch contained and isolated. The risk is that toggling between fake and real timers mid-test could confuse React 18's scheduler, but it's a contained approach. Though I'm realizing the DEV gate might actually be false on this machine due to NODE_ENV being set to production in the shell, which means `landed()` wouldn't trigger the reduced-motion path anyway — so the helper might be solving the right problem for the wrong reason. Setting `process.env.NODE_ENV = 'test'` at the top of vitest.config.ts before defineConfig runs would make DEV true consistently across machines, aligning with the existing env configuration. I should search the codebase for other uses of `import.meta.env.DEV` to see if flipping it true in tests would have unintended side effects elsewhere.

I'm noticing the header wrapper uses `pointer-events-none` to disable interactions, then re-enables them on inner elements with `pointer-events-auto`. The key issue is that Chromium's draggable region computation ignores `pointer-events`, so the gradient scrim below the header—which is 40 pixels tall and spans the full width—might still be registering as a draggable region even though it shouldn't be interactive.

Actually, `-webkit-app-region` isn't inherited in CSS, so the draggable region is computed geometrically as the union of all elements marked with `app-region: drag`, minus any elements marked `app-region: no-drag`. This means the header's full box becomes a drag region, then subtracts the nav, right cluster, and logo boxes from that area.

The left span with the empty space isn't marked `app-no-drag`, so that area stays draggable — which is intentional. The nav and right cluster are both excluded, so their buttons should be clickable. Popovers and tooltips render to the body outside the header, so they won't interfere with the drag region itself.

But there's a real macOS bug here: the header has `z-40`, and while the z-index ladder puts popovers at `z-[70]`, the `-webkit-app-region` property completely ignores z-index. The drag region is just a flat geometric union, so z-stacking doesn't matter for it.

This means anything drawn over the header — a toast, dialog, popover, or panel — sits visually above it but the header's drag region still covers that same rectangle at the OS level. Since the macOS drag overlay NSView sits above all web content, clicking on a toast or dialog that overlaps the top 70px gets intercepted by the drag region and triggers a window drag instead. That's exactly what he's describing — sometimes the header elements feel unclickable because the macOS chrome is interfering.

So the header elements themselves are inside `app-no-drag` boxes, but they'd become unclickable if the drag regions are stale. Actually, I'm recalling that Electron switched around v13 to a different approach — instead of an overlay view, they check if a click lands in the drag region during `mouseDown` and perform the window drag directly. I need to trace through how the renderer handles the tray route, check the tray panel component and icon definitions, and look at the entry point. I also want to see if there's already a settings or profile menu in place, how localStorage is being used for settings, and examine the `useCrew` hook's `sendChat` function to understand the LLM integration — particularly for the cleanup feature where the user wants to remove filler words and improve grammar.

The cleanup could be done with local rules or through the LLM, but since the user specified "using your LLMs," I'm thinking this runs through the local agent CLI. That said, there's a performance concern — the full Wispr Flow experience needs to be fast: hold hotkey, talk, release, transcribe, clean up, and paste. The user wants filler removal (um, uh), self-correction handling ("scratch that"), and grammar fixes, all while keeping it snappy. I'm also noting a technical blocker: Fn key on macOS can't be captured by Electron's `globalShortcut` since it's handled at a lower system level — I'd need to use CGEventTap to intercept it. On Windows, bare modifier keys like Ctrl or Win alone can't be registered with Electron's `globalShortcut` — it needs a non-modifier key paired with it. So both platforms require a low-level keyboard hook beyond what `globalShortcut` offers. I'm settling on `uiohook-napi` since it's a maintained N-API binding that gives global keydown/keyup events for modifiers, which is exactly what push-to-talk needs. I'll flag the Fn key uncertainty on macOS and suggest Right Option or Right Cmd double-tap as a fallback.

For pasting the transcribed text into another app, I need to write to the clipboard and then send Cmd+V or Ctrl+V to the focused window. Electron can't synthesize system-wide key events natively, but `uiohook-napi` exposes `keyTap` which can handle this. Let me first check if `uiohook-napi` is already in the dependencies and what else is available.

I could also use `osascript` on macOS or PowerShell `SendKeys` on Windows to avoid native dependencies, but those are slower (~100ms for osascript) and clunky. Better to stick with one consistent approach using `uiohook-napi`.

The tricky part is keeping the pill window from taking focus — if it steals focus, the target app loses it and the paste goes to the wrong place. The window needs to be non-focusable but still clickable for the X and check buttons, which requires careful handling of mouse events and focus behavior.

For the latency issue with whisper-base.en on WASM, I should leverage WebGPU in transformers.js (Electron supports it) and stream audio in chunks so transcription happens while the user is still talking, leaving only the tail to process on release. For quality, whisper-small.en or distil-whisper would be better locally than the base model.

For cleanup, I'm thinking of a two-layer approach: first, a local rule-based pass that handles filler words, self-corrections like "scratch that," spoken punctuation, and capitalization—this is instant and deterministic. Then optionally an LLM pass through the crew's agent for polish, but that adds latency, so I'd make it off-by-default and clearly flag the performance cost.

Actually, there's a better middle ground: the crew already has agents, but sending to the CLI for cleanup is a full prompt round trip that takes 2-5 seconds and kills the responsiveness feel. So rules by default, with "Polish with an agent" as an opt-in toggle in settings. Whisper's own prompt settings can help with punctuation and capitalization too—the base model already handles those reasonably well.

For naming, I need something short and Crew-like. The app uses plain names—Toolbox, Huddles, Voice, Music, Games, Docs, Boards, Flow. Since Crew already has "Voice," I need something different. Options like "Whisk," "Quill," "Say," "Speak," or "Mic" are possibilities, but I'm still weighing what fits best.

Leaning toward **Scribe** as a noun—it's plain, one word, and says exactly what it does: the person who writes down what's said. That reads well as a tile in the toolbox. I'll propose Scribe with Quill and Ink as alternates, keeping the copy simple and clear for everyone, not just engineers.

For the pill UI, I'm building it with Crew's glass styling and strong variant, rounded pill shape, and an InsetRing. The bars are drawn directly onto elements the way the existing bars component does it, and I'm using Crew's glyphs for the X and check—the outlined X on the left and solid white check on the right to match the screenshot.

Now I'm thinking about voice activity detection. The user asked for a repo that's good at tracking voice, which points to VAD. Silero VAD is the state-of-the-art small model, and `ricky0123/vad-web` wraps it as an ONNX model for the browser—1.8MB, runs in a worklet, way better than an RMS gate at distinguishing speech from background noise. Crew's current `VoiceGate` is just an RMS gate, which works but isn't speech-aware. For push-to-talk specifically, VAD isn't critical since the hotkey already brackets the utterance, but it helps with the animated bars, trimming silence before sending to Whisper, and a few other things.

So the plan is to keep `VoiceGate` for the bars and add Silero via `@ricky0123/vad-web` or raw onnxruntime for the endpointing logic—and I should be clear that this is optional and can be phased in. Now I need to check the package.json dependencies, the icons list, Bars.tsx, and how the tray routing works. I should also verify whether `@huggingface/transformers` webgpu is viable given the CSP constraints, which apparently needs `wasm-unsafe-eval` and `worker-src blob:` according to AGENTS.md.

The `applyPlatform()` function runs synchronously before the first render, so the `mac` class gets applied immediately. For the fullscreen state, I'm checking how `window.crew.onWindowShape` works — the main process publishes the shape through events like `enter-full-screen`, `leave-full-screen`, and `maximize`. This means a fresh window or reload starts with `full = false` by default, which is correct. But there's a problem: if the app is already fullscreen and the renderer reloads, the `full` flag stays false instead of reflecting the actual window state.

I'm stepping back to focus on what I can actually verify. The most likely culprits are: whether the main process calls `setWindowButtonVisibility`, and whether there are any overlays sitting on top of the header's drag region. Let me search the main process for window shape handling and anything that might be interfering.

Actually, I keep thinking about a well-documented Electron bug on macOS where `-webkit-app-region: no-drag` regions become stale when an element's rect changes without the actual set of draggable regions changing. The `DraggableRegionsChanged` event only fires from the compositor when the regions themselves change, not when they move or resize.

There's also a more commonly reported macOS issue where clicks near the top of the window get consumed after a window drag or when the app-region overlay view exists. Rather than trying to reproduce this programmatically (which wouldn't work since `sendInputEvent` bypasses OS-level hit-testing), I should identify the most probable cause by reading the code carefully and then suggest what Jamel should test. Let me focus on proving the concrete overlap problem by examining the code directly.

The header spans the full window width at 70px height with carve-outs only for `nav`, the right cluster, and `CrewLogo`. Several overlays could be floating over this band — `TasksPanel` is the critical one since it's absolutely positioned across the full height including that top 70px band, though it does declare `app-no-drag` to carve out its own region. I need to check whether its parent overlay is properly handling the drag region, and then verify how `SidePanel`, `HuddlePanel`, and `VoiceScreen` interact with the header's drag zone.

The real issue is that `app-no-drag` carve-outs from hidden or covered elements still punch holes in the drag region, and `app-drag` from covered elements still make the window draggable — so when Settings opens as a full takeover, the top band underneath can still drag the window because TopBar remains mounted beneath it, creating dead spots where the nav carve-out exists but the overlay blocks interaction.

But Jamel's complaint is specifically about not being able to click header elements. Let me think about what's actually layered over the header — the Toaster sits at z-45 positioned on the right side, and looking at App.tsx line 103, there's an absolutely positioned overlay div with `pointer-events-none` that contains the top bar container with `pointer-events-auto`. The parent container is `pointer-events-none` and spans the full viewport, so when the panel is closed and translated off-screen, it doesn't interfere with interactions. When open, it covers the top-right area including the header, but since it's marked `app-no-drag`, it just overlays what's already there without causing issues.

Let me actually look at the remaining files and the main process code to see what's happening. I think the key might be how `-webkit-app-region: drag` works on macOS in Electron — the drag region swallows mouse events and triggers window dragging, and Chromium recomputes it on the compositor thread whenever a paint happens that changes it. The `.top-bar-container` has `container-type: inline-size` which applies size containment...

Actually, let me step back and focus on what's testable and fixable. Jamel mentioned macOS Chrome getting in the way, so let me reconsider the traffic-lights theory more carefully by looking at the actual geometry.

The window has `titleBarStyle: 'hiddenInset'` with traffic lights positioned at `{x: 20, y: 27}`. With `hiddenInset`, macOS creates a titlebar container view that spans the full window width—Electron implements this using `NSWindowStyleMaskFullSizeContentView` with a transparent titlebar, and the actual inset traffic lights come from adding an `NSToolbar` to the window.

In Electron 33, this toolbar makes the titlebar area roughly 52–60px tall and full width, which means native toolbar views intercept clicks and window interactions like double-click zoom and drag-to-move. With `TOP_BAR_H = 70` and 40px buttons centered vertically (occupying y = 15..55), the toolbar band at y = 0..52 overlaps the button area, so I need to account for that interaction zone.

But wait—if only the bottom 3px of each button is clickable, that would make them nearly impossible to interact with, not just "sometimes" unresponsive. The issue might be more nuanced: `trafficLightPosition` only works with `titleBarStyle: 'hidden'` in newer Electron versions, while `hiddenInset` has its own positioning rules and doesn't respect that setting the same way.

Rather than keep debugging the traffic light positioning, the real solution is to flip the approach entirely: make the drag region explicit and minimal instead of making the whole header draggable and carving out exceptions. That directly solves the "sometimes can't click" problem—right now, anything not explicitly marked `app-no-drag` inside the `app-drag` region becomes unclickable, including overlays from elsewhere in the DOM and gaps that shift as the layout reflows.

Checking the structure: the logo has `app-no-drag`, the nav is wrapped in `app-no-drag`, and the right side controls are in an `app-no-drag` div. Everything looks covered. The `PresenceStack` renders inline within an `app-no-drag` container, so that's fine too.

Wait — what if something's layering on top of the header? The Toaster positioning could be the culprit. If it's positioned at `top-4 right-4` instead of `top-[70px] right-4`, it would overlap the right cluster of header controls. Toasts appear and disappear dynamically, which would explain the "sometimes" behavior. And if the toast card has pointer-events enabled for hover interactions, it would intercept clicks meant for the Toolbox, Tasks, or Avatar buttons underneath.

+ // Everything a generated picture is worked out from: an id, which decides the
+ // picture, and the colors it is photographed in. A track carries both, and so
+ // does a helper's mark, which is why this stands here rather than in the music.
+ 
+ export interface CoverSubject {
+   id: string
+   colors: readonly string[]
+ }
+ 
+ // Nothing in a palette is dark and nothing but the light is a near white. The
+ // darkest place in a picture like this is a color in shade, never an ink, and a
+ // shape pale enough to have no color left in it stops being a thing in the frame
+ // and becomes a hole cut in it.
+ const SHELVES: ReadonlyArray<readonly [string, string, string, string, string]> = [
+   ['#ff8fa8', '#ffc09f', '#8fd4e8', '#fff2e8', '#f56b8a'],
+   ['#8ce68f', '#a0e88f', '#ffd98f', '#f2fff4', '#7fd4f0'],
+   ['#8fb8ff', '#b0c9f5', '#ffc9a8', '#f4f8ff', '#4f8ef5'],
+   ['#c48fff', '#d4b0ff', '#9ff0d8', '#faf2ff', '#a87ae8'],
+   ['#ffc85c', '#ffd07a', '#8fc4f0', '#fff8e6', '#f5943c'],
+   ['#5fe0f0', '#94e0f5', '#ffbf9f', '#eefbff', '#3fa8e0']
+ ]
+ 
+ // A palette that is always the same for the same seed, so everyone's screen
+ // shows the same picture and two of them are told apart at a glance.
+ export function paletteFor(seed: string): readonly string[] {
+   let hash = 0
+   for (let i = 0; i < seed.length; i++) hash = (hash * 31 + seed.charCodeAt(i)) >>> 0
+   return SHELVES[hash % SHELVES.length]
+ }
+ 
+ // A number in 0..1 from a seed and a word for what is being asked, so one id can
+ // answer a dozen questions without any two of them moving together.
+ export function seeded(id: string, of: string): number {
+   let hash = 2166136261
+   const text = `${id}�${of}`
+   for (let i = 0; i < text.length; i++) {
+     hash ^= text.charCodeAt(i)
+     hash = Math.imul(hash, 16777619)
+   }
+   return ((hash >>> 0) % 100000) / 100000
+ }

This means overlays like Modal, ScreenPicker, and VoiceScreen that float above the header visually still sit beneath the drag region geometrically, so clicking in the top 70px of those overlays triggers a window drag on macOS instead of interacting with the control. I'm working through the positioning of the close button in the settings modal—on taller windows the card centers nicely, but on shorter viewports around 600px height, the card sits much higher up, which pushes the close button dangerously close to the top edge.

Now I see the real issue: the Tasks panel scrim is covering the header entirely because it's positioned as `absolute inset-0` with a z-index that paints over everything. The fix needs two parts—first, the scrim should sit below the header so clicks on the header buttons still work while clicks on the body close the panel. Looking at the z-index ladder, the header is at z-30/z-40 and panels are z-50, so the scrim should be z-30 to stay underneath.

But there's a pointer-events subtlety: the header wrapper is `pointer-events-none` with only the bar itself and buttons set to `pointer-events-auto`, so clicks on the gradient strip fall through to the scrim below, which closes the panel. The Tasks button itself currently closes the panel through the scrim eating the click, which works by accident—the button's onClick never fires because the scrim intercepts it first.

Now for the drag region issue: on macOS, `-webkit-app-region` ignores z-index and pointer-events, so any overlay drawn over the header band has its clicks swallowed into a window drag. The better approach is to disable the drag region entirely when a modal or takeover is open, rather than trying to carve out draggable zones around the gaps.

Actually, the cleanest solution is to add `app-no-drag` to the root of each floating primitive — Modal, ScreenPicker, Popover, Tooltip, HoverCard — so they automatically carve themselves out of the header's drag region regardless of z-index. That's one class per primitive, fixes it permanently, and aligns with the reusable primitives philosophy. Let me check which ones already have it and add it where needed.

For fixed inset-0 elements like Modal and ScreenPicker, adding `app-no-drag` will correctly prevent dragging the window while they're open, which is the right behavior. I need to verify that `-webkit-app-region: no-drag` on portaled body-level elements properly subtracts from the header's drag region — and it does, since the region is computed globally across the document in order.

Chromium walks the layout tree collecting draggable regions, adding or subtracting each element's border box in paint order. Since portaled overlays are appended to the body after the app root, their subtractions happen after the header's additions, so the math works out correctly.

For Tooltip specifically, I need to be careful about which element gets `app-no-drag` — the wrapper around the trigger or the floating label itself. The wrapper would carve out the trigger (which is usually already no-drag), so I should apply it to the floating label instead. Let me check the actual component files.

+ import { seeded } from '../../../../shared/art'
+ import { CIRCLE, GRID, SOLID } from '../../icons/keylines'
+ 
+ // The silhouette a helper's mark is seen through, worked out from its id the way
+ // a cover's scene is. It is kept apart from the drawing for the same reason: a
+ // generator like this is held to its rules by a test, and a test cannot read a
+ // canvas.
+ 
+ export type ShapeKind = 'rosette' | 'disc' | 'square' | 'hexagon'
+ 
+ export interface SubagentShape {
+   kind: ShapeKind
+   // How many lobes stand out around a rosette. Nothing else has any.
+   lobes: number
+   // How far they stand out, as a share of the mean radius.
+   depth: number
+   // The whole shape turned, so two roles with the same count are still two
+   // marks.
+   twist: number
+   // The mean radius, which every kind holds to. That is what makes a flower and
+   // a disc weigh the same beside each other: the eye reads the average of an
+   // outline, not the furthest point of it.
+   radius: number
+ }
+ 
+ export const MIN_LOBES = 3
+ export const MAX_LOBES = 8
+ 
+ // A solid form carries its whole box as ink where an outlined one carries only
+ // its edge, so it sits under the square keyline. The round family is 8.8% wider
+ // than the square one at every size, which is the one thing that has to travel
+ // with it or a disc reads small beside a tile.
+ const ROUND = (SOLID * CIRCLE) / 17
+ const SQUARE_SIDE = SOLID
+ 
+ // More lobes at the same depth is a smaller waist between each pair, so how far
+ // they may stand out comes down as they multiply. Past this the mark reads as
+ // scattered dots at 18 across rather than as one shape.
+ const deepest = (lobes: number): number => 0.34 - (lobes - MIN_LOBES) * 0.026
+ 
+ // A page of flowers is a page of flowers. The covers hold the same rule with
+ // their six casts, and it is what stops every mark being the same picture in a
+ // different color.
+ function kindOf(id: string): ShapeKind {
+   const roll = seeded(id, 'kind')
+   if (roll < 0.72) return 'rosette'
+   if (roll < 0.82) return 'disc'
+   if (roll < 0.91) return 'square'
+   return 'hexagon'
+ }
+ 
+ export function subagentShape(id: string): SubagentShape {
+   const kind = kindOf(id)
+   const lobes = kind === 'rosette' ? MIN_LOBES + Math.floor(seeded(id, 'lobes') * (MAX_LOBES - MIN_LOBES + 1)) : 0
+   const depth = kind === 'rosette' ? 0.12 + seeded(id, 'depth') * (deepest(lobes) - 0.12) : 0
+   return {
+     kind,
+     lobes: Math.min(lobes, MAX_LOBES),
+     depth,
+     twist: seeded(id, 'twist') * Math.PI * 2,
+     radius: (kind === 'square' ? SQUARE_SIDE : ROUND) / 2
+   }
+ }
+ 
+ export function radiusAt(shape: SubagentShape, angle: number): number {
+   if (shape.kind !== 'rosette') return shape.radius
+   return shape.radius * (1 + shape.depth * Math.cos(shape.lobes * (angle + shape.twist)))
+ }
+ 
+ const SAMPLES_PER_LOBE = 10
+ 
+ const at = (shape: SubagentShape, angle: number, box: number): [number, number] => {
+   const r = (radiusAt(shape, angle) / GRID) * box
+   return [box / 2 + Math.cos(angle) * r, box / 2 + Math.sin(angle) * r]
+ }
+ 
+ const round = (n: number): number => Math.round(n * 1000) / 1000
+ 
+ // Closed with quadratics through the midpoints, the way the pet's body is, so
+ // nothing anywhere in the set has a corner in it that was not asked for.
+ function smooth(points: Array<[number, number]>): string {
+   const mid = (a: [number, number], b: [number, number]): [number, number] => [(a[0] + b[0]) / 2, (a[1] + b[1]) / 2]
+   const count = points.length
+   let path = `M ${mid(points[count - 1], points[0]).map(round).join(' ')}`
+   for (let i = 0; i < count; i++) {
+     const next = points[(i + 1) % count]
+     path += ` Q ${points[i].map(round).join(' ')} ${mid(points[i], next).map(round).join(' ')}`
+   }
+   return `${path} Z`
+ }
+ 
+ // The outline as a path on a box of the size it is asked for, so the one shape
+ // answers the mark, the clip and the sheet without any of them knowing how it
+ // was worked out.
+ export function shapePath(shape: SubagentShape, box: number = GRID): string {
+   const half = box / 2
+   const unit = (r: number): number => (r / GRID) * box
+   if (shape.kind === 'disc') {
+     const r = round(unit(shape.radius))
+     return `M ${round(half - r)} ${round(half)} a ${r} ${r} 0 1 0 ${round(r * 2)} 0 a ${r} ${r} 0 1 0 ${round(-r * 2)} 0 Z`
+   }
+   if (shape.kind === 'square') {
+     const side = unit(shape.radius * 2)
+     const x = round(half - side / 2)
+     // A squarer corner than the app's cards wear. This is a mark rather than a
+     // surface, and a heavily rounded square at 18 across is a disc.
+     const r = round(side * 0.28)
+     return `M ${x} ${round(half)} a ${r} ${r} 0 0 1 ${r} ${round(-side / 2)} h ${round(side - r * 2)} a ${r} ${r} 0 0 1 ${r} ${r} v ${round(side - r * 2)} a ${r} ${r} 0 0 1 ${round(-r)} ${r} h ${round(-(side - r * 2))} a ${r} ${r} 0 0 1 ${round(-r)} ${round(-r)} Z`
+   }
+   if (shape.kind === 'hexagon') {
+     const points = Array.from({ length: 6 }, (_, i) => at(shape, shape.twist + (i / 6) * Math.PI * 2, box))
+     return `M ${points.map(point => point.map(round).join(' ')).join(' L ')} Z`
+   }
+   const count = shape.lobes * SAMPLES_PER_LOBE
+   return smooth(Array.from({ length: count }, (_, i) => at(shape, (i / count) * Math.PI * 2, box)))
+ }

step.text:
I'm settling on the name Scribe for this tool—it's a single word that clearly describes the function, and it creates a nice distinction from Voice, which already exists in Crew for agent conversations. Scribe captures the idea of transcribing what you say into written form.

For the architecture, I'm deciding between two approaches: either the pill window handles everything (the microphone, the worker, the transcription model, and the UI), or the main window does the audio work while the pill just displays. The first option means the model loads twice if both windows are open, but since they're separate renderers and the browser caches the model, the second load comes from disk. The second option is cleaner in theory but breaks the tool when the main window closes, which defeats the purpose of a dictation tool that works everywhere. I'm going with the first approach—the pill window becomes the complete Scribe interface, running on the `#scribe` route like the tray panel, pre-warmed at startup with the whisper model already loaded so the first keystroke is instant.

The tricky part is keeping the pill from stealing focus. On Windows, `focusable: false` still allows mouse events in Electron, but on macOS I need `setAlwaysOnTop(true, 'screen-saver')` with a panel type and `showInactive()` to display without focusing. The real problem is that clicking the pill on macOS would activate the app and steal focus from whatever I'm trying to dictate into. The solution is to use a non-activating panel type—on macOS that's `NSWindowStyleMaskNonactivatingPanel`, which Electron exposes through the `type: 'panel'` option in BrowserWindow.

I'll use `type: 'panel'` on macOS and `focusable: false` on Windows, though I need to verify clicks still register on the buttons. As a backup, I could have the main process remember the frontmost app before showing the pill and re-activate it before pasting, but that's getting complex—I'll note it as an option if the simpler approach doesn't work.

Now for the hotkey approach, which has three tiers depending on what dependencies I'm willing to add.

The first tier is `globalShortcut` with standard key combos like `Ctrl+Cmd+Space` on Mac and `Ctrl+Win+Space` on Windows for toggle mode—this ships in phase 1 with no new dependencies.

The second tier is bare-modifier push-to-talk, where the user just holds Fn on Mac or Ctrl/Win on Windows. That requires a low-level keyboard hook since Electron's `globalShortcut` can't register a modifier alone, and Apple doesn't expose Fn in the public API. I'd use `uiohook-napi` for global keydown/keyup events on modifiers. The main risk to check early is whether it actually works reliably with Electron.

For the paste feature, I'm writing the text to the clipboard and then sending a paste keystroke to the focused window, which I can do with the same hook library.

macOS also requires an Accessibility permission prompt on first launch, which needs to be documented in settings.

The performance chain needs to be optimized: key release triggers whisper transcription, then cleanup, then paste. The model should load when Scribe arms rather than on first keypress, and the UI window should warm up at startup like the tray panel does. I'm considering whether to keep the mic open continuously or open it only when armed — an always-open mic creates a visible indicator that might concern users.

The real challenge is the mic initialization latency. `getUserMedia` takes 100-300ms cold, which clips the start of the first word. I could keep the `AudioContext` and worklet alive between sessions, but the honest tradeoff is opening the mic when Scribe arms and keeping it muted so nothing is heard, then enabling the track on keydown. The catch is that even with muting, macOS still shows the recording indicator. The alternative is accepting ~150ms of latency on keydown and requiring the key to be held briefly to mask that delay.

I'll go with opening on keydown and offering a setting for users who want zero latency and don't mind the indicator showing. That's a transparent choice to present.

For the model itself, WebGPU gives 5-10x speedup over wasm when available, which transforms a 20-second dictation from feeling like a beat to taking a second and a half. I'm also planning chunked transcription in phase 3—every 4 seconds of held key, transcribe the accumulated audio in the background so only the tail remains when the key releases. That's what makes long dictations feel instant. Since `whisper-base.en` is already downloaded by Crew, there's no extra cost there.

For cleanup, I'm building a shared utility function that handles the parts users actually care about—removing fillers like "um," "uh," "erm," and bracketed filler phrases, plus handling self-corrections where the user says things like "scratch that" or "no wait" to delete back to an earlier point.

I'm also handling spoken punctuation markers like "period" or "new line" that get converted to actual punctuation, though I'll make the explicit ones like "new paragraph" on by default and gate the ambiguous ones like "period" behind a setting to avoid mangling phrases like "the period after the war." Beyond that, I'm normalizing sentence structure with proper capitalization and spacing, collapsing immediate word repetitions, and supporting a personal dictionary for terms Whisper consistently mispronounces.

There's an optional LLM polish pass that runs through a fast local model rather than a full agent, but I'm recommending it stay off by default since the rule-based pass is the real product and the LLM adds latency without much benefit for a dictation tool.

For the UI, I'm building the control bar with an X button in a dark circle on the left, a check in a white circle on the right, and bars connecting them—using a glass-strong pill style with an inset ring and close glyph.

The bars themselves should pull directly from the microphone's frequency bands, drawing low frequencies on the left up to high frequencies on the right, just like the music visualization. I'm extracting the bar-drawing logic into a shared primitive that accepts a levels function, so both the music and Scribe components can reuse it without duplicating the per-frame rendering.

For the settings, I'm adding a new Scribe tab to the existing Settings modal with its own glyph. Since Voice already uses MicGlyph and the toolbox needs a distinct icon, Scribe warrants its own unique mark drawn through the crew-icons system.

Scribe is entirely local to this machine—the hotkey, mic, model, and dictionary all stay in localStorage with nothing synced to the crew or event log, matching how terminals work.

For the file structure, I'm starting with `src/shared/scribe.ts` as the core module that handles settings (hotkey mode, paste/copy behavior, filler removal, punctuation, dictionary entries), applies the cleaning passes for self-correction and punctuation handling, and keeps everything pure without external dependencies.

Then `tests/scribe-tidy.test.ts` validates the whole pipeline with concrete examples—removing filler words like "um" and "uh", handling self-corrections like "scratch that", preserving intentional phrases, and applying dictionary replacements.

Finally, `src/main/scribe-keys.ts` manages the global hotkey registration and emits state changes to listeners... The paste utility handles clipboard operations with a platform-specific branch, swapping text in and out. The main process wires everything together: creates the scribe window, sets up IPC handlers for settings and completion events, and sends key press signals to the pill. The preload and environment types expose the bridge functions for the renderer to trigger dictation, handle results, and resize the window. Finally, I'm building the audio capture module that opens a microphone track, runs it through the same worklet and resampling logic the voice ear uses, collects all samples, and returns them as a single buffer.

Rather than duplicate the audio processing pipeline, I'll reuse the existing listen worker which already converts one utterance to text—just swap in WebGPU with a wasm fallback, which benefits the voice screen too.

Next I need a new Zustand store to track the scribe's lifecycle: whether it's off, hearing, reading, done, or failed, plus managing the take, listener, cleanup, and handoff to the main thread. Then I'll build the UI pill component with close button, level bars, and confirmation check, pulling the bar visualization into a shared `Levels` primitive that the music player can also use.

The scribe window becomes its own full-page view routed at `#scribe`, similar to how `TrayPanel` works. In the main router, I'll replace the nested ternary with a cleaner routing table to handle the three-way branch between tray, scribe, and default views.

For settings, I'm adding a dedicated scribe panel with toggles for on/off and tidying options, hotkey configuration (mode and key selection), post-transcription behavior (paste or copy), dictionary management with editable rows, and a microphone picker that reuses the existing device menu component.

The scribe tile goes into the toolbox—it lights up when armed and opens the scribe settings when clicked. I'm also creating a scribe glyph icon and adding it to the icon test suite, plus writing tests for the audio capture path using a fake worklet similar to the voice suite tests.

Phase 2 focuses on the real hotkey system using `uiohook-napi` with postinstall scripts for binary handling, ASR unpacking, the accessibility prompt on macOS, and teaching the settings page to record key presses. Phase 3 will handle chunked transcription while the key is held and keep the mic ready, using Silero VAD to trim silence before sending audio to Whisper for better accuracy and speed, plus an optional agent polish pass.

I'm also planning a `yarn scribe-check` script following the `voice-check` precedent—something that can catch a broken listener by running the real model against real speech and pressing the actual hotkey. For CSP, WebGPU doesn't need anything extra since we already have `wasm-unsafe-eval` and `worker-src blob:`, though I need to check if the VAD library loads its own wasm module.

I'll need to bundle the VAD model locally instead of fetching from a CDN to stay within Crew's rule that nothing reaches the internet except the models we already pull. On macOS, I should verify the entitlements file has `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and add `NSAppleEventsUsageDescription` if we use osascript for paste, plus check that the hardened runtime includes `com.apple.security.device.audio-input`.

For the recording modes, the user wants three behaviors: hold to record and release to finish, toggle mode where you press once to start and again to stop, and a latch mode where a quick tap locks recording on until you tap again—which is Wispr's approach and feels the most natural. I can unify this with a single setting using a hold threshold around 250ms: if you release under that time it latches, over that time it ends the recording. Escape and the X button both cancel. I'll propose the latch as the default and keep the documentation plain and readable without em dashes or semicolons.

Now I'm organizing the implementation plan file by file, presenting Scribe as the primary name choice with two alternatives noted briefly since the user asked for one recommendation. I'll lay out the open questions clearly at the end so they can make decisions, keeping the whole thing detailed but concise.
The typecheck passes, and I should check the `window-chrome.test.ts` file since it might be the right place to add this rule.
